"If, O Disciples of the Buddha!

the Bodhisattva’s ground of the nature of the Flower Adornment Body of the Buddha, by means of the Buddha’s majestic deportment, enters and emerges from the Tathāgata’s Samādhirāja-samādhi at no fixed time, attaining Buddhahood, turning the Wheel of Dharma, and even entering parinirvāṇa simultaneously throughout the ten directions, within the three thousandfold world-systems, across ten billion suns and moons and ten billion sets of four continents."

All Buddha-activities are manifested simultaneously for all sentient beings within a single mind; all physical bodies possess the eighty minor marks and thirty-two major signs with sovereign mastery, delighting in emptiness as being identical to space.
With immeasurable great compassion, adorned with the marks and signs of radiance, they are neither devas nor humans, nor beings of the six realms.

Yet, while remaining outside all dharmas, they constantly traverse the six realms, manifesting immeasurable bodies, immeasurable speech, and immeasurable minds, and preaching immeasurable Dharma gates. They are able to transform the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddha, and the realm of the Buddha into the realm of Māra; furthermore, they transform all views into the Buddha-view, and the Buddha-view into all views; the Buddha-nature enters the nature of sentient beings, and the nature of sentient beings enters the Buddha-nature.

That ground is radiant with light; it is illumined by wisdom, illumined by insight, and ablaze with the flames of clarity. It is fearless, immeasurable, and possesses the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, liberation, nirvana, and the single path of unconditioned purity.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings as one's own parents and brothers, one preaches the Dharma for them until the end of all kalpas so that they may attain the fruits of the Way.

Moreover, one manifests in all lands, regarding all sentient beings as one would look upon a father or a mother, and regarding even celestial Māras and followers of external paths as one would look upon a father or a mother.

Abiding in this stage, from the limit of birth and death up to the adamantine limit, one manifests such events within a single thought-moment and is able to enter into the realms of immeasurable sentient beings.
Such immeasurable [qualities] are, in brief, like a single drop in the ocean.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva enters the ground of the essential nature of the Buddha-realm, their great wisdom is empty; it is empty, then further empty, and again empty, like the nature of space."

The wisdom of equality possesses the *tathāgatagarbha*, being fully endowed with the ten qualities of merit; it is empty and of a single characteristic, its essence being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Its spiritual power is void and its substance is one, identical with the *dharmatā* of all phenomena; therefore, it is called the Tathāgata.

One who accords with the Four Truths and the Two Truths, reaches the limit of the cycle of birth and death, and maintains the Dharma-body through the nourishment of the Dharma without duality, is called an Arhat (Worthy of Offerings).

One who pervades all matters within all worlds, possessing correct wisdom and noble liberating wisdom, and who knows the existence and non-existence of all phenomena as well as the faculties of all sentient beings, is the Samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfectly Enlightened One).
Because his clear and manifest cultivation is sufficient for the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, he is the "One Perfect in Clarity and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasampanna).

He has well departed through the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time; his Dharma is identical to that of the Buddhas who preceded him and those who have gone before. Because he was excellent when departing and excellent when arriving, he is named the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata).

This person practices these supreme virtues and enters into the world to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from all fetters; therefore, he is called the "Liberator of the World."

This person enters the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power upon all dharmas; their deportment and form are like those of the Buddha, and they abide in the sphere of practice of a Great Being (mahāsattva). For the sake of the liberation of the world, they are called the Unsurpassed One (anuttara-puruṣa).
One who harmonizes and disciplines all sentient beings is called a "great man" (mahāpuruṣa).

Because he teaches and transforms all sentient beings among devas and humans, and because they consult him and receive his words of Dharma, he is the Teacher of Devas and Humans (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām).

The wondrous source is non-dual; the Buddha-nature is profound awakening, eternally and ever-present in great fulfillment. Because all sentient beings pay homage and show reverence, they are the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Because all people consult it, receive it, and revere its teachings, it is the stage of the Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*).
Because it is the place entered by all sages within this stage, it is called the stage of the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātubhūmi*).
At that time, seated upon a precious lotus flower, all were filled with joy at receiving their prophecy.
The Dharma-body hand stroked their crowns, and bodhisattvas who had seen the same and studied together praised this non-duality with one voice.

Furthermore, all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas from hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds gathered like clouds at once, requesting that he turn the ineffable Dharma-wheel and the Dharma-gate of the space-treasury’s transformative guidance.

This stage contains unspeakably wondrous dharma-gate chapters, including marvelous gates of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), samādhi, and dhāraṇī; these are not known by the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings in lower stages, but only the immeasurable body, speech, and mind of Buddha after Buddha can exhaustively fathom their source.
As it is said in the *Ābhāsvara-deva-parivarta*: "The ten fearlessnesses are identical with the Buddha-way.
From the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, Volume One, the Preface to the Bodhisattva Precepts: "O sons of the Buddhas!..."
Join your palms and listen with a sincere mind.
I now wish to recite the Preface to the Great Precepts of all Buddhas.
The assembly having gathered, listen in silence.
Those who know they have committed an offense should confess; through confession, there is peace and happiness, whereas through non-confession, the offense becomes deeper.
Those without offense should remain silent; by their silence, it should be known that the assembly is pure.
"Venerable upāsakas and upāsikās, listen attentively.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, you should revere the Prātimokṣa; the Prātimokṣa is precisely these precepts."

When upholding these precepts, it is like encountering light in darkness, like a poor person finding treasure, like a sick person recovering from illness, like a prisoner released from jail, or like a long-distance traveler returning home.
You should know that this is the Great Teacher of the assembly; it is no different from the Buddha dwelling in the world.
It is difficult for a sense of dread to arise and difficult for a wholesome mind to be generated; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Do not disregard even a small offense, thinking there will be no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel."
"In a single kṣaṇa one may commit a sin that leads to falling into the Avīci Hell; once lost, this human body will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas.
Vigorous youth does not linger, like a galloping horse; human life is as impermanent as flowing water or mountain torrents; though one exists today, even tomorrow cannot be guaranteed."

May each of you cultivate with single-minded diligence and vigor; be careful not to be indolent, lazy, or given over to sleep, nor to indulge your own whims. At night, collect your mind and maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Do not let this pass in vain by merely setting up empty toil, lest you deeply regret it in future generations.
Each of you, with single-mindedness, should carefully rely upon these precepts and practice according to the Dharma; this is how you should train.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra, Spoken by Vairocana Buddha, Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva Ground Precepts,
Part Two of the Lower Volume.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened the *Cittabhūmi* (Mind-Ground) from among the dharma-gates of the hundred thousand Ganges-sands of ineffable teachings, [revealing it] to the extent of a single hair-tip:

"This has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, will be taught by the Buddhas of the future, and is being taught now by the Buddhas of the present; it is what the Bodhisattvas of the three periods have studied, will study, and are studying now."
"I have cultivated this ground of the mind for a hundred kalpas and am named Rocana.
You, all Buddhas, shall turn what I have spoken and open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings."
At that time, from the blazing celestial light upon the lion throne in the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury World, Rocana Buddha emitted rays of light and addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals:

"Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground' and go; furthermore, for the sake of the thousands, hundreds, and billions of Śākyamunis and all sentient beings, teach this 'Chapter on the Supreme Mind-Ground Dharma-Gate' in successive order."
"You all should receive, uphold, read, and recite this, and practice it with single-minded devotion.

At that time, the Buddhas of the thousand petals and the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis rose from their majestic lion thrones in the Lotus Treasury World; each withdrew, emitting inconceivable light from their entire bodies, and from that light were manifested immeasurable Buddhas.

At that time, they made offerings of immeasurable blue, yellow, red, and white flowers to Vairocana Buddha; having completed the reception and upholding of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as previously taught, each of them vanished from this Lotus Treasury World.

Having passed away, he entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Essential Nature of Emptiness; returning to the world of Jambudvīpa beneath the Bodhi tree at its source, he emerged from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Essential Nature of Emptiness.
Having emerged, he sat upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne and, in the Hall of Sublime Light, expounded the ten oceans of worlds.
Rising again from his seat, he proceeded to the palace of Śakra and expounded the ten stages (bhūmi).
Again rising from his seat, he went to the Yāma Heaven and expounded the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).
Again rising from his seat, he went to the fourth heaven (Tuṣita) and expounded the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
Again rising from his seat, he went to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and expounded the Ten Meditative Concentrations (*daśa-dhyāna*).
Again, he rose from his seat and went to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) to expound the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Again, he went into the First Dhyāna to expound the Ten Vajras; again, he went into the Second Dhyāna to expound the Ten Patiences (*daśakṣānti*); again, he went into the Third Dhyāna to expound the Ten Vows (*daśapraṇidhāna*); and again, he went into the Fourth Dhyāna, to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, to expound the Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground as taught by Rocana Buddha in my own source, the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*).
The remaining thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are likewise thus, without duality or distinction, as described in the "Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpika-parivarta).

At that time, after Śākyamuni Buddha had first appeared from the Lotus Treasury World in the east and entered the palace of the Heavenly King to preach the *Sūtra on the Demon’s Conversion*, he descended to be born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in Jambudvīpa; his mother was named Māyā and his father was called Śuddhodana.
My name is Siddhārtha; I left home at the age of seven and attained the Way at thirty, and am thus called Śākyamuni Buddha.
From sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne at the Site of Enlightenment until reaching the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, [I have taught this Dharma].
This was taught sequentially within the tenth dwelling place.

At that time, the Buddha observed the net-bannered staff (*jāla-dhvaja*) of the Great Brahmā Kings and, on that account, explained that immeasurable worlds are like the mesh of a net; each and every world is distinct and different in its immeasurable variety, and the gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so.

I have now come to this world eight thousand times; for the sake of this Sahā world, I have sat upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne, even unto the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, and have finished briefly expounding the Chapter on the Dharma Gate of Opening the Mind-Ground for all the great assembly therein.

Furthermore, descending from the palace of the Heavenly King to the Bodhi tree beneath the Jambūdvīpa, for the sake of all sentient beings upon this earth—those ordinary persons shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—he preached the light of the single precept that was constantly recited by me, Vairocana Buddha, when first awakening the mind within the Heart-ground.
The Vajra Jewel Precepts are the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of Buddha-nature.

All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; all consciousnesses, forms, and minds—whether emotional or cognitive—are entirely subsumed within the precepts of Buddha-nature. Because there is always a cause for each and every instance, there is the eternally abiding Dharma-body for each and every instance.
Thus, these ten *prātimokṣa* emerge in the world; they are the dharma-precepts, which all sentient beings of the three periods of time receive, uphold, and honor upon their heads.

I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly, again expound the chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasury Precepts, which are the fundamental source and intrinsically pure nature of the precepts for all sentient beings.
"I, now Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal;
Upon the thousand surrounding flowers, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis.
Within each flower are ten billion lands, And in each land is one Śākyamuni."
Each sits beneath a Bodhi tree, attaining the Way of Buddhahood simultaneously.
Thus, the thousands of kotis of Śākyamunis, who are the very body of Vairocana,
each receive as many beings as there are atoms of dust.
All come together to my presence to hear me recite the Buddha’s precepts;
the gate of ambrosia is then opened.
Returning to their original places of practice, each sits beneath a Bodhi tree.
I shall now recite the precepts of my original teacher:
The precepts are like the sun and moon, And also like a string of precious jewels;
By means of them, the multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, Attain perfect enlightenment.
This is what Vairocana recites; I too recite it in this same way.
You, newly initiated bodhisattvas, should receive and uphold these precepts upon the crown of your heads.
Having received and upheld these precepts, you shall in turn transmit them to all sentient beings.
Listen attentively as I correctly recite the treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma, the Prātimokṣa;
let the great assembly believe it with a sincere heart.
You are those who shall become Buddhas; I am one who has already become a Buddha.
Always maintain such faith, and the precepts will be fully perfected.
All sentient beings who possess a mind should receive the Buddha's precepts;
when sentient beings receive the Buddha's precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
"Having attained a rank equal to Great Enlightenment, you are truly the sons of all Buddhas;
the great assembly shall all pay you respect, so listen with a sincere heart as I recite.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unsurpassed enlightenment, first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa:

"Be filial and obedient toward your parents, preceptors, teachers, and the Triple Gem; be filial toward the Dharma of the Ultimate Way. Filiality is called the precepts, and it is also called restraint.
As he spoke, the Buddha emitted immeasurable light from his mouth.

At that time, a great assembly of ten trillion bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmā deities, the sons of the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm, and sixteen great kings joined their palms with single-minded devotion and listened as the Buddha recited the Mahayana precepts of all Buddhas.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Every half-month, I myself recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas.

You all, bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds, should also recite them; even the bodhisattvas of the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis should likewise recite them."
Therefore, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth; it has conditions and is not without cause.

This light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black; it is neither form nor mind, neither existent nor non-existent, and is not a phenomenon of cause and effect. It is the original source of all Buddhas, the foundation of Bodhisattvas, and the root of the great assembly of all Buddha-sons.

Therefore, the great assembly of all Buddha-sons should uphold, recite, and study this well. Listen attentively, O Buddha-sons! Whether one receives the Buddha-precepts as a king, prince, high official or minister;

a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī; one of the eighteen Brahmā heavens or a son of the six heavens of desire; a commoner, eunuch, lecherous man or woman, or slave; a member of the eight classes of ghosts and spirits, or a *vajra* deity; an animal, or even a transformed person—provided they understand the words of the Dharma Master, all may receive the precepts and are called the foremost pure ones.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas, saying:
"There are ten grave *pratimokṣa* precepts. If one receives the Bodhisattva precepts but does not recite these precepts, they are not a Bodhisattva, nor are they a seed of the Buddha."
I likewise recite this: all bodhisattvas have studied it, all bodhisattvas shall study it, and all bodhisattvas are now studying it.
Having briefly explained the characteristics of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa, one should train in these matters and uphold them with a reverent heart.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha!
Whether one kills by oneself, instructs others to kill, employs skillful means to praise killing, rejoices upon seeing it being done, or even kills through incantations."
Regarding the causes of killing, the conditions for killing, the methods of killing, and the karmic acts of killing—down to all living beings—one must not intentionally kill them.

This Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of constant compassion and filial obedience, employing skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings. If, however, they kill with a self-indulgent mind and a sense of pleasure, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the Bodhisattva.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

Whether you steal yourself, teach others to steal, or employ skillful means to steal; whether through the causes of stealing, the conditions for stealing, the methods of stealing, or the karmic actions of stealing—including stealing by incantations, or even taking the property of spirits and deities that have an owner, or the goods of bandits—one must not intentionally steal any material thing, not even a single needle or a blade of grass."

If a bodhisattva, who ought to give rise to a mind of filial piety, compassion, and kindness toward the Buddha-nature, and who should constantly assist all people in generating merit and happiness, instead steals another's wealth and property, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that bodhisattva.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Whether committing adultery oneself or instructing others to do so, one must not intentionally engage in sexual misconduct with any woman whatsoever.

This includes all causes of lust, conditions for lust, methods of lust, and karmic acts of lust—even with female animals, female devas, female ghosts, or female spirits—and even engaging in sexual intercourse through improper orifices."

Furthermore, a bodhisattva ought to give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, and to purify the Dharma for others; yet if, on the contrary, they further incite all people to sexual misconduct, without distinguishing even among animals, even committing incest with their own mother, daughter, sister, or other six types of close relatives, being devoid of a compassionate heart—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

To speak falsehoods oneself, to teach others to speak falsehoods, or to employ skillful means for speaking falsehoods; the causes of falsehood, the conditions for falsehood, the methods of falsehood, and the karma of falsehood—even to say one has seen what one has not seen, or to say one has not seen what one has seen—constitutes falsehood of body and mind."

If a bodhisattva constantly gives rise to right speech and right view, and causes all sentient beings to give rise to right speech and right view, yet conversely further incites all sentient beings to engage in wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions, this constitutes a pārājika offense for that bodhisattva.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

To sell alcohol oneself, or to teach others to sell alcohol—whether through the causes of selling alcohol, the conditions of selling alcohol, the methods of selling alcohol, or the karmic actions of selling alcohol—one must never sell any kind of alcohol; for such alcohol gives rise to the causes and conditions of transgression.”

If a bodhisattva should give rise to the wisdom of clear insight for all sentient beings, yet instead gives rise to the minds of perversion in all sentient beings, this constitutes a pārājika offense for that bodhisattva.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If one personally speaks of the transgressions of ordained or lay bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, or bhikṣuṇīs, or teaches others to speak of their transgressions—the causes of the transgressions, the conditions of the transgressions, the dharmas of the transgressions, and the karmic actions of the transgressions."

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing non-Buddhists, evil persons, or those of the two vehicles speak of what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya within the Buddha-dharma, consistently gives rise to a heart of compassion and teaches these evil people so as to cause them to produce wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna; yet, if that bodhisattva instead speaks of faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma themselves, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the bodhisattva.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

To praise oneself and disparage others, or to teach others to praise themselves and disparage others—this constitutes the cause for disparaging others, the condition for disparaging others, the method for disparaging others, and the karma of disparaging others.”

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva should take upon himself all the insults and humiliations suffered by all sentient beings, directing evil toward himself and giving good to others. If he instead proclaims his own virtues, conceals the good deeds of others, and causes others to suffer humiliation, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva.
“O Sons of the Buddha! To be stingy oneself,
or to teach others to be stingy— whether through the causes of stinginess, the conditions of stinginess, the methods of stinginess,
or the karmic actions of stinginess— if a Bodhisattva sees any poor person coming to beg, they should give whatever that person requires.

If, however, a bodhisattva, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, fails to give even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass; and if, when there is one who seeks the Dharma, they do not explain even a single word, a single verse, or a portion of the Dharma as small as a mote of dust, and instead further reviles and insults them, this constitutes a pārājika offense for that bodhisattva.
“O Sons of the Buddha! To be angry oneself,
or to teach others to be angry— whether through the causes of anger, the conditions of anger, the methods of anger, or the karmic actions of anger—
a Bodhisattva should instead cultivate roots of goodness and non-contention among all sentient beings, and always give rise to a heart of compassion.”

If, on the contrary, one reviles and insults all sentient beings—even those who are not sentient beings—with harsh speech, and further strikes them with the hand or attacks them with blades and staves without ceasing; and if, even when the other person seeks reconciliation and offers sincere apologies with kind words, one’s anger remains unresolved, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

To slander the Triple Gem oneself, or to teach others to slander the Triple Gem—whether through the cause of slander, the conditions for slander, the dharma of slander, or the karma of slander—is a grave offense.
When a Bodhisattva hears even a single word of slander against the Buddha from a non-Buddhist or an evil person, it is as if three hundred spears were piercing his heart.”

How much more so if one personally slanders [the Dharma] with no faith or filial heart, yet instead assists evil people and those with wrong views in their slander; this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"O virtuous ones who have studied well!
This is the ten-fold Prātimokṣa of the Bodhisattva; you should study it.
Within it, you must not commit even a single transgression so small as a mote of dust, much less commit all ten precepts in their entirety."

If there are those who commit such offenses, they shall not be able to give rise to the bodhicitta in their present bodies; they shall also lose the status of a king or a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), as well as the status of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī. They shall also lose the wondrous fruit of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature—the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten grounds—and they shall lose everything.
Falling into the three evil realms, for two or three kalpas they shall not hear the names of their parents or the Three Jewels.
For this reason, one must not transgress each and every precept.
All you bodhisattvas—those who have studied, those who are now studying, and those who will study hereafter—should train in these ten precepts and uphold them with a reverent heart.
"The Chapter on the Eighty Thousand Modes of Deportment shall explain this in detail.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"The ten *pratimokṣa* rules have now been fully expounded; the forty-eight minor precepts shall now be explained."
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha!

When one desires to receive the position of a king, when one receives the position of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), or when the various officials receive their positions, one should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts."
All ghosts and spirits shall protect the person of the King and the persons of his officials, and all Buddhas shall rejoice.

Having received the precepts, one should give rise to a mind of filial piety and reverence; upon seeing elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), great fellow students, or those of like view and practice, one should rise to welcome them, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being.

Yet the Bodhisattva, on the contrary, gives rise to a mind of arrogance, conceit, and delusion; he does not rise to welcome him or pay homage, nor does he provide each requisite offering according to the Dharma, even though he could do so by selling his own body, his kingdom, his city, his sons, his daughters, his seven treasures, and all manner of goods to provide for him.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense of defilement.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!
If one intentionally drinks alcohol, it gives rise to immeasurable faults and transgressions."
If one passes a vessel of wine with one's own hand to another to drink, one shall be born without hands for five hundred lifetimes, let alone drinking it oneself.
One must not instruct any person to drink, nor cause any sentient being to drink wine, much less drink it oneself.
If one intentionally drinks [alcohol] oneself or teaches others to drink it, one commits a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!
If one intentionally eats meat..."

No meat whatsoever may be eaten; it cuts off the seed of the nature of great compassion, and all sentient beings will see [the eater] and depart. Therefore, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being; eating meat incurs immeasurable offenses.
If one intentionally eats them, one commits a minor offense.
"O disciples of the Buddha! You must not eat the five pungent roots: [garlic, leeks, onions, scallions, and asafoetida]."
Garlic, leeks, scallions, onions, and water lily bulbs—
these five kinds may not be eaten among any foods.
If one intentionally eats them, one commits a minor offense.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If you see any sentient beings who have violated the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts; who have broken prohibitions, committed the seven heinous crimes, or fallen into the eight difficulties—all such offenses of violating the precepts—you should teach them to perform repentance."

If a bodhisattva does not instruct another to repent, yet dwells with them, shares the same monastic provisions, and participates together in the *poṣadha*—reciting the precepts within the same assembly—without exposing their offenses and teaching them to reform, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
If you see a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, a fellow student of the Mahāyāna, or those who share the same views and practices, entering a monastery, a private residence, or a city;”
If anyone comes from a hundred or a thousand *li*, he immediately rises to welcome them and sees them off, prostrating and making offerings.

He makes offerings three times every day, spending three *jin* of gold daily on food, a hundred flavors of delicacies, bedding, seats, and medicine to serve the Dharma Master, providing him with everything he requires.

He constantly invited the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day, and every day he performed prostrations during those three periods; without giving rise to anger or a mind of resentment, he was willing to sacrifice his own body for the sake of the Dharma, never ceasing in his quest for the teachings.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

Wherever the Vinaya-sūtras and Vinaya-piṭakas are being expounded—whether in a great residence or at a place where the Dharma is taught—a newly initiated Bodhisattva should carry the volumes of the sūtras and vinaya to the Dharma Master’s location to listen, receive instruction, and inquire about them."
Whether in mountain forests, beneath trees, on monastic grounds, or within rooms—whenever there is a place for the preaching of the Dharma, one must go to all such places to listen and receive it.
If one does not go to those places to listen and receive it, one commits a minor offense.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If one turns the mind away from the Mahāyāna, claiming that the sūtras and vinaya which are eternally present were not spoken by the Buddha, yet instead accepts and upholds the two vehicles of the śrāvakas, the evil views of external paths, or any prohibitions, precepts, or sūtras of false views, one commits a light secondary offense."
"O Sons of the Buddha!

Upon seeing anyone who is ill, you should always provide for them with offerings no different from those given to the Buddha; among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of caring for the sick is the foremost field of merit."
If one's parents, teachers, monastics, or disciples fall ill—suffering from impaired faculties or the afflictions of a hundred types of disease—one must care for them until they recover.

If a Bodhisattva, out of an evil mind or resentment, fails to go to a monastery or encounter and rescue those who are sick within cities, towns, wildernesses, mountains, forests, or on the roads, they commit a minor offense.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

You must not possess any swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, axes, or other implements for combat; nor any evil nets, snares, or instruments for killing living beings. You must not possess any of these at all."
Furthermore, even if a Bodhisattva were to be killed by their own parents, they would not seek retribution; how much less so toward any other sentient beings.
If one intentionally keeps any kind of blade or staff, one commits a minor offense.
"These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind.
They shall be explained in detail within the following six chapters.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“O Son of the Buddha!

One must not, for the sake of gain or with an evil mind, serve as a messenger between nations to coordinate military arrays, raising armies to strike one another and slaughter immeasurable sentient beings.”
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva must not enter an army to come and go, much less intentionally act as a traitor to the state.
If one does so intentionally, they commit a minor secondary offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

Therefore, one should not trade in free persons, slaves, or livestock, nor in coffins, planks, or wood for funerary implements used to contain the dead; one should not do these things oneself, much less teach others to do so.
If one intentionally commits this, they incur a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

If, out of an evil mind, one groundlessly slanders a virtuous person, a good person, a Dharma Master, a teacher-monk, a king, or a noble official, saying that they have committed one of the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses."

Toward one's parents, siblings, and six kinds of relatives, one ought to give rise to a mind of filial piety and compassion; yet, if instead one further commits acts of hostility and harm, causing them to fall into undesirable states, one incurs a minor offense of defilement.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
If, out of an evil mind, you set a great fire to burn mountains, forests, or wilderness;

or from the fourth month until the ninth month, you set fire to the houses, dwellings, cities, monasteries, fields, or timber of others, as well as the property of spirits or the state—none of these things belonging to an owner may be intentionally burned."
If one intentionally burns [the scriptures], one commits a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

Toward fellow disciples of the Buddha, as well as followers of external paths, the six types of relatives, and all spiritual friends, you should teach each and every one of them to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sutras and vinaya. You should teach them to understand the principles and meanings, causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta, the ten minds of development, the ten minds of nurturing, and the ten adamantine minds."
Within the thirty minds, one must understand each of their sequential methods and applications.

Yet, if a Bodhisattva, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, arbitrarily teaches others the sūtras and vinayas of the Two Vehicles—the Śrāvakas—or the heterodox and false views of non-Buddhist treatises, they commit a light secondary offense.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
You should, with a sincere heart, first study the Mahāyāna Vinaya and Sūtras regarding dignified conduct, extensively opening up and understanding their meanings and essences.

When you see newly initiated Bodhisattvas who have come from as far as a hundred or a thousand li to seek the Mahāyāna Vinaya and Sūtras, you should, in accordance with the Dharma, explain for them all forms of ascetic practice, such as burning the body, burning the arms, or burning the fingers.”
If one does not burn one’s own body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, one is not a renunciant bodhisattva.

One should even sacrifice one’s own body, flesh, hands, and feet to provide for hungry tigers, wolves, lions, and all hungry ghosts; thereafter, one should explain the True Dharma to each of them in turn, so that their minds may be opened and their intentions liberated.

If a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and offerings, fails to answer when they ought to, or explains the words of the sutras and vinaya in a distorted manner without proper sequence, or slanders those who preach the Triple Gem, they commit a minor offense.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

If, for the sake of food, drink, money, material gain, or reputation, you draw near to kings, princes, ministers, and officials, relying on their power and influence to beg, seize, beat, or drag others, and thus take money and goods by force or seek all manner of profit, this is called ‘evil seeking.’”
"To seek much for oneself and to teach others to seek it, while entirely lacking a heart of compassion and a heart of filial obedience, constitutes a minor offense.
"O disciples of the Buddha!
Those who study and recite the precepts must uphold the Bodhisattva precepts during the six periods of day and night, and understand their underlying principles—the nature of the Buddha-nature."

If a bodhisattva does not understand the causes and conditions of even a single phrase or a single verse of the precepts, yet falsely claims to understand them, they are deceiving themselves and also deceiving others.
If one does not understand any of the dharmas themselves, yet acts as a teacher for others and bestows the precepts upon them, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

If, out of an evil mind, you see a precept-keeping bhikṣu holding an incense burner while practicing the bodhisattva path, and you instead instigate strife between two parties, slandering and deceiving that worthy person, there is no evil you will not commit."
If one intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

Out of a heart of compassion, you should practice the act of releasing living beings. All men have been my fathers, and all women have been my mothers; throughout my successive lives, there has never been one from whom I did not receive birth. Therefore, the sentient beings of the six realms are all my parents."
Those who kill and eat [living beings] are killing my own parents and are also killing my former body.
All earth and water were my previous bodies, and all fire and wind are my original substance; therefore, one should always practice the release of living beings.
One should teach others to release living beings, for this is the Dharma of constant abiding through successive births.

When one sees people of the world killing animals, one should employ skillful means to rescue and protect them, liberating them from their suffering and hardship; one should constantly instruct and preach the Bodhisattva Precepts in order to save and deliver all sentient beings.

On the day of the death of one's parents or siblings, one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra to provide merit for the deceased, so that they may behold the Buddhas and be reborn among humans or in the heavens.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart; the specific characteristics of each precept are explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Extinction of Offenses."
The Buddha said, “Son of the Buddha!
One must not repay anger with anger, nor repay a blow with a blow.”
If one kills one's parents, brothers, or other members of the six categories of kin, one must not seek retribution.
If the sovereign of a state is killed by another, one likewise must not seek retribution.
To kill in order to provoke a retaliatory killing does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety.

One should not even keep slaves, nor beat, strike, or revile them; for every day, one commits immeasurable verbal offenses through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind—how much more so the intentional commission of the seven heinous crimes.
If an ordained Bodhisattva lacks compassion and seeks revenge, even against those among their six kin, and intentionally retaliates, they commit a minor offense.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

When you have first left the household life and have not yet attained any understanding, yet you rely on your own cleverness and intelligence; or you rely on your noble status, your advanced age, or your birth in a great clan of high standing; or you rely on your great erudition, your great merit, and your abundance of wealth and the seven treasures—through such arrogance, you refuse to consult or receive the sutras and vinaya from senior Dharma masters.”
As for that Dharma Master, he may be of humble lineage and young, from a lowly family and poor, with impaired faculties; yet in reality he possesses virtue and understands all the sūtras and vinayas.

If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not inquire about or receive instruction from a Dharma Master regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) because they judge the Dharma Master’s lineage, they commit a minor offense (āpatti).
“O Sons of the Buddha!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when one with a sincere and virtuous mind wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, and takes the vow to receive them before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, one must perform repentance before the Buddha for seven days. Upon seeing a favorable sign, one then attains the precepts.”
If one does not obtain an auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*), one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to one year, until an auspicious sign is obtained.
Once the auspicious sign has been obtained, one may then receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.
If one does not obtain a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*), even if one receives the precepts before an image of the Buddha, one does not obtain the precepts.
However, if one has previously received the Bodhisattva precepts in the presence of others, it is not necessary to see a favorable sign when receiving the precepts before a Dharma Master.
Why is this? Because these Dharma masters have transmitted it from teacher to teacher, there is no need for auspicious signs.
Therefore, when a Dharma master receives the precepts before [the assembly], he immediately obtains them; because he generates a mind of profound respect, he thereby attains the precepts.
If within a thousand li there is no master capable of bestowing the precepts, one may receive them before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, provided that one awaits a favorable sign.
If a Dharma Master relies on his own mastery of the sutras, vinaya, and Mahayana teachings to study the precepts, he may act as a virtuous friend to kings, crown princes, and high officials.

If a newly initiated bodhisattva comes to inquire about the meaning of the sutras or the meaning of the vinaya, and one responds to each question with a light mind, an evil mind, or a mind of pride rather than answering well, one commits a minor offense.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

If there are the Buddha’s sutras and vinaya, the Mahayana True Dharma, right view, right nature, and the True Dharma-body, yet one fails to diligently study and practice them, instead abandoning the seven treasures to study the false views of the two vehicles, external paths, secular classics, the Abhidharma, miscellaneous treatises, and historical records—this is to sever the Buddha-nature and create the causes and conditions for obstructing the Path; it is not the practice of the Bodhisattva path.”
If one intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor transgression.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who serve as masters of preaching the Dharma, masters of monastic dwellings, masters of instruction and transformation, masters of seated meditation, or masters of administrative affairs, should give rise to a heart of compassion and skillfully reconcile disputes. They must skillfully guard the property of the Triple Gem and must not use it recklessly as if it were their own."
Yet, if one instead disturbs the assembly, engages in strife and contention, and recklessly uses the property of the Triple Gem, one commits a minor offense of defilement.
"If, O Disciple of the Buddha!

you were previously residing in a monastic dwelling, and later see visiting Bodhisattvas or Bhikṣus entering a monastic dwelling, a residence, a city, the palace of a king, or even a place for summer retreat or a great assembly; [and you do not welcome them with respect]..."
The resident monks should welcome them upon arrival and see them off at their departure, providing food and drink, as well as rooms, bedding, and rope-seated couches;
they should provide for every necessity. If they lack material goods, they should even sell themselves, their sons, or their daughters to provide for them, giving whatever is required.

If a donor comes to invite the assembly of monks, and there are guest monks entitled to a share of the offerings, the master of the monastery should assign the guest monks to receive the invitation in due order.
If the resident monks alone accept the invitation without assigning the guest monks, the master of the monastery incurs immeasurable transgression.
"To keep livestock is no different from being neither a śramaṇa nor of the Śākya clan.
If one does so intentionally, they commit a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).
"O Disciples of the Buddha!..."
One must not accept special invitations for offerings and take them for oneself; rather, such offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions.
To accept a special invitation is to take the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for one's own use.
Regarding the eight fields of merit— the Buddhas, the sages, each of one’s teachers and preceptors, parents, and the sick—
one commits a minor offense by using their property for oneself.
"If a disciple of the Buddha!..."

When ordained bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, and all donors wish to invite the Sangha as a field of merit to make offerings and seek their aspirations, they should enter the monastic quarters and inquire with the administrative officers.
If one now wishes to invite them according to the sequential order of the Sangha, one thereby obtains the assembly of worthy and holy monks from the ten directions.
Yet, the worldly practice of separately inviting five hundred Arhats and Bodhisattvas is not equal to inviting a single ordinary monk according to the sequence of the Sangha.
If one invites the Sangha individually, this is the practice of non-Buddhists.
Among the Seven Buddhas, there was no method for individual invitations, as it does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety.
If one intentionally invites the Sangha individually, one commits a minor offense.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If, out of an evil mind or for the sake of profit and sustenance, you engage in the sale of men and women for sexual purposes; if you prepare food with your own hands, grind or husk grain yourself; if you practice physiognomy on men and women, interpret dreams for good or ill fortune, determine whether a fetus will be male or female, employ incantations and arts, or train hawks; if you compound a hundred kinds of poisons, a thousand kinds of poisons, snake venom, 'living gold' (mercury), or spirit-induced poisons—doing all these things without a single heart of compassion."
If one intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

If, out of an evil mind, one slanders the Triple Gem oneself, feigning intimacy while claiming to speak of emptiness yet acting within the realm of existence, and acting as a go-between for laypeople to facilitate sexual intercourse and attachment to lustful desires."

On the six days of fasting and during the three months of the long fast each year, those who commit acts of killing, robbery, or violate the fast and transgress the precepts incur a minor offense of defilement.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart.
"It is explained in detail within the Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts. The Buddha said,
"O Son of the Buddha!"

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this evil age, if one sees non-Buddhists or any wicked people, robbers, or thieves who sell images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one’s parents; who trade in the sūtras and the Vinaya; or who sell bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as those bodhisattva-practitioners who have resolved their minds for enlightenment, making them serve as officials or enslaving them as slaves to all manner of people.
When a bodhisattva sees such matters, they should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, employing skillful means to rescue and protect them, and teaching and transforming others everywhere.
They should use their own property to ransom Buddha and Bodhisattva images, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds on enlightenment, and all sūtras and vinayas.
If one does not redeem them, one commits a minor offense.

"O Disciples of the Buddha! You must not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows; you must not trade with light scales or small measures; you must not seize the property of others by relying on official authority or power; you must not, with a harmful intent, bind or destroy successful works; and you must not raise cats, ferrets, pigs, or dogs."
If one intentionally commits these acts, one incurs a minor transgression.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

Out of an evil mind, you must not observe the fighting of men and women, nor the battles of armies, generals, or bandits. Furthermore, you must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, *konghou* lutes, singing, shouting, or musical performances. You must not play *chupu*, *weiqi*, *bolosai*, *dani*, *liubo*, ball games, stone-throwing, *touhu*, the eight-path city game, or practice divination using claw-mirrors, milfoil stalks, willow branches, alms bowls, or skulls. You must not act as a messenger for thieves; none of these things shall be done."
If one intentionally commits such an act, one incurs a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!
To uphold the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you should recite these precepts during the six periods of day and night."
One should be like a vajra; like one carrying a life-preserving float wishing to cross the great ocean; or like a bhikṣu bound by grass.
One should constantly give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, knowing for oneself: "I am a Buddha-to-be," while all Buddhas are Buddhas who have already attained completion.
"Generate the bodhicitta and let it never depart from your mind for even a single thought-moment.
If you give rise to a single thought of the two vehicles or of non-Buddhist paths, you commit a minor offense.
"If you, O Disciple of the Buddha!"
One should always bring forth all vows: to be filial and obedient toward one’s parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem;

to wish for the attainment of a good teacher, fellow students, virtuous friends, and spiritual mentors who constantly instruct one in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, the ten stages of setting forth (*daśa-prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*daśa-poṣadha*), the ten adamantine stages (*daśa-vajra*), and the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), so that I may attain understanding and practice according to the Dharma while firmly upholding the Buddha’s precepts.
One would rather sacrifice body and life than let this [vow] depart from the mind for even a single thought-moment.
If any Bodhisattvas do not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
"O disciples of the Buddha!..."
Having made these ten great vows, he upholds the prohibitions and precepts of the Buddha, making this aspiration:

"I would rather cast this body into a great pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of blades than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman."
"Furthermore, he makes this vow:
'I would rather have my body encircled on all sides by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than ever, with a body that has broken the precepts, accept any clothing from a faithful donor.'"
Furthermore, he makes this vow:

"I would rather swallow hot iron balls and great streams of fierce fire with this mouth for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever use a mouth that has broken the precepts to eat the food of a hundred flavors offered by a faithful donor."
Furthermore, he made this vow:

"I would rather lie with this body upon a floor of hot iron meshed with fierce, raging flames than ever accept a hundred kinds of beds and seats from a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts."
"Furthermore, he makes this vow:

'I would rather have this body endure the piercing of three hundred spears for one or two kalpas than ever, with a body that has broken the precepts, accept the medicinal offerings of a hundred flavors from a faithful donor.'"
Furthermore, he made this vow:

"I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of boiling iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever, with a body that has broken the precepts, accept the thousand kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, groves, fields, and lands offered by faithful donors."
Furthermore, he made this vow:

"I would rather have this body smashed from head to foot with an iron hammer until it is reduced to fine dust than ever accept the respectful prostrations of a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts."
Furthermore, he makes this vow:
"I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by a hundred thousand heated iron swords and spears than ever look upon the beautiful forms of others with a mind that violates the precepts."
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"I would rather have my ears pierced all over with a hundred thousand iron awls for the duration of one or two kalpas than ever listen to pleasant sounds with a mind that has broken the precepts."
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"I would rather have my nose cut off with a hundred thousand sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances."
"Furthermore, he makes this vow:
'I would rather have my tongue cut off by hundreds of thousands of blades than ever, with a mind that has broken the precepts, eat the hundred-flavored pure food of others.'"
"Furthermore, he makes this vow:
'I would rather have my body hacked and cut with a sharp axe than ever, with a mind that has broken the precepts, crave pleasant tactile sensations.
He further makes this vow:"
"I vow that all sentient beings shall fully attain Buddhahood.
If a bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
"O disciples of the Buddha!..."
One should always practice the *dhūta* austerities during the two seasons; one should practice *zazen* (seated meditation) in winter and summer, and observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

One should always maintain: a willow branch and cleansing powder; the three robes, a water flask, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, and a mendicant’s staff; an incense burner and a water-strainer; a hand towel and a small knife; a fire-starter and tweezers; a rope bed; and the *sūtras*, the *vinaya*, as well as images of the Buddha and bodhisattvas.
When a bodhisattva practices the dhūta austerities or travels abroad, whether traveling a hundred or a thousand *li*, these eighteen items always accompany his person.

The period for practicing the dhūtas is from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month.
During these two periods, these eighteen kinds of items constantly accompany his body like the two wings of a bird.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, the newly initiated bodhisattva performs the *poṣadha* every half-month and recites the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
At that time, before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, if there is one person performing the *poṣadha*, that one person shall recite it;
whether there are two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand people, only one person shall recite it.
The reciter sits on a high seat, while the listeners sit on lower seats.
Each person dons the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya*.
They observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in every detail according to the Dharma.

When practicing dhūta, do not enter dangerous places. Whether it be national turmoil or a wicked king; terrain that is uneven with deep grasses and thickets; dangers from lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, or wind; or bandits on the road and venomous snakes—do not enter any such dangerous places whatsoever.
If one is practicing the dhūta austerities, or even observing the summer retreat (varṣā), one must not enter any of these dangerous places.
If one enters them intentionally, one commits a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
“O Sons of the Buddha!
You should sit according to the proper sequence of the Dharma.

Those who received the precepts first shall sit in front; those who received the precepts later shall sit behind. Regardless of age—whether old or young—and regardless of status—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, nobles, kings, princes, or even eunuchs and slaves—all should sit with those who received the precepts first in front, and those who received the precepts later seated in successive order behind them.”
"It is not like the foolish practitioners of external paths, who—whether old or young—sit without precedence or sequence according to the law of soldiers and slaves.
In my Buddha-dharma, those who come first sit first, and those who come later sit later."
If a Bodhisattva does not sit in the proper order, they commit a minor offense.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
You should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings."

One should establish monastic quarters, mountain forests, gardens, and fields, and construct stūpas for the Buddha; likewise, one should establish places for winter and summer retreats, sites for seated meditation, and all locations for the practice of the Path.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings. Whether during times of illness, national calamities, or threats from bandits; on the day of the passing of one’s parents, brothers, preceptors (upādhyāya), or teachers (ācārya); or during the periods of seven days up to forty-nine days—on these occasions, one should likewise recite, chant, and expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya. This should also be done during vegetarian assemblies to seek merit, or when traveling or engaging in livelihood.

When one is threatened by a great conflagration, swept away by a great flood, blown off course by a black wind while aboard a ship, or faces the perils of rākṣasas upon rivers, streams, or the great ocean, one should likewise recite, chant, and expound this sutra and vinaya.

Even for all karmic retributions—whether the three types of retribution, the seven heinous offenses, or the eight difficulties; whether one's body is bound by cangues, shackles, or pillories; or if one suffers from excessive lust, anger, ignorance, or many illnesses—one should read, recite, and expound this sutra and its vinaya.
If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not act accordingly, they commit a minor offense.
These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart.
They shall be explained in the "Chapter on the Brahma-Altar."
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha!
When bestowing the precepts upon others, one must not engage in discrimination."

All kings, princes, ministers, and officials; bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; faithful men and women; male and female libertines; the eighteen Brahmā devas; the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire; those without sexual organs, those with double organs, eunuchs, and slaves; and all ghosts and spirits—all may receive the precepts.

One should instruct that all the saṃghāṭī robes worn on the body be dyed in discolored hues to accord with the Way; all robes should be dyed in blue, yellow, red, black, or purple, and even bedding and requisites should all be of discolored colors, so that every garment worn on the body is dyed in such colors.
In whatever country one may be, the robes worn by a bhikṣu must differ from the secular clothing of the people of that land.
When one wishes to receive the precepts, the preceptor should ask:
"Have you not committed any of the seven heinous offenses in this present life?"
"A Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not bestow the precepts upon those who have committed the seven heinous offenses in their present life.

The seven heinous offenses are: shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing one's Upādhyāya, killing one's Ācārya, disrupting the Saṃgha that performs the *karmavācanā* or turns the wheel of the Dharma, and killing an Arhat."
If one possesses the seven obstructions (*saptāvaraṇa*), one cannot receive the precepts in this present life; all other persons may fully receive them.

According to the dharma for those who have left the household life, one does not prostrate to kings, nor does one prostrate to parents; one does not show reverence to the six types of relatives, nor offer salutations to ghosts or spirits; one need only understand the words of the teacher.

If there are those who come from a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma, yet the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind, does not immediately bestow the precepts for all sentient beings upon them, he commits a minor offense.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When instructing others to give rise to faith, a Bodhisattva acting as a preceptor and teacher for another must, upon seeing one who wishes to receive the precepts, instruct them to request two masters:
a *upādhyāya* and an *ācārya*.
The two masters should ask:
"Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses?
If the candidate currently has any of the seven obstructing offenses, the masters should not confer the precepts upon them; one who is free from the seven obstructing offenses may receive them.
If there are those who have violated the ten precepts, they should be instructed to perform repentance.
Before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, they should recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts during the six periods of the day and night.

If one practices with utmost sincerity, worshipping the thousand Buddhas of the three periods, one will attain a vision of a "good sign. Whether it takes seven days, two or three weeks, or even up to a year, one must eventually see such a good sign.
Regarding auspicious signs: if the Buddha comes to touch one’s head, or if one sees various extraordinary signs such as light or flowers, one will then be able to extinguish one’s transgressions.
If no auspicious signs appear, then even though one performs repentance, it will be of no benefit.
Such a person cannot receive the precepts in their present body, yet they may receive them through further ordination.
If they violate the forty-eight minor precepts, their offenses are extinguished through confession before another; this is not the same as the case of the seven prohibitions.
Yet, within these teachings, the instructor must understand each point thoroughly.

If they do not understand the characteristics of what is light or heavy, and what is right or wrong, regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya; if they do not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), nor the nature of the seeds of practice (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*), the nature of nourishment (*āpyāyana-gotra*), the indestructible nature (*anupaccheda-gotra*), the nature of the path-seeds (*mārga-bīja-gotra*), or the true nature (*bhūta-gotra*); and if they do not understand the various degrees of contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), the entry into and emergence from the ten factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*), or any of the dharmas of practice—they shall fail to grasp the essential meaning within these teachings.

Yet, for the sake of gain and fame, such bodhisattvas seek and greedily crave disciples through improper means; they falsely pretend to understand all the sūtras and vinayas, and for the sake of offerings, they deceive themselves and deceive others.
Therefore, to transmit the precepts to others [under such circumstances] constitutes a minor offense (light dust-offense).
"O Sons of the Buddha!

For the sake of profit and sustenance, you must not preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts, nor before non-Buddhists or evil persons."
One must not speak [of this] before those with wrong views; except for the king, it must not be spoken to anyone else.
Such wicked people do not receive the Buddha’s precepts and are called "beasts."

If one fails to perceive the Triple Gem throughout successive lifetimes, being as heartless as wood or stone, such a person is called a follower of external paths with heterodox views, no different from a block of wood.
If a Bodhisattva preaches the seven teachings and precepts of the Buddha before such an evil person, they commit a minor offense.
“O sons of the Buddha!

If one has left the household life with faith and received the authentic precepts of the Buddha, yet then gives rise to the thought of violating these sacred precepts, they shall not receive the offerings of any donors; nor shall they walk upon the ground of the king, nor drink the water of the king. Five thousand great ghosts will constantly block their path.”
The ghost says,
"Great thief! If he enters a room, a city, or a house, the ghost constantly sweeps away his footprints.
All people of the world revile him, saying:
"A thief within the Buddha-dharma.
All sentient beings do not wish to see him with their eyes.
A person who violates the precepts is no different from an animal and no different from a block of wood.
If one destroys the right precepts, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
"If, O Disciple of the Buddha!..."
One should always single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas;
even if one must flay one's own skin to serve as paper, draw blood for ink, use marrow as water, and split one's bones to serve as pens, one should transcribe the Buddha’s precepts.
One should also write and maintain [the scriptures] upon tree bark, grain husks, paper, silk, bamboo, and cloth.
One should always use the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to fashion caskets and bags to contain the volumes of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
If one makes offerings that do not accord with the Dharma, one commits a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!
You should constantly give rise to a heart of great compassion."
If one enters any city, town, or dwelling and sees any sentient beings, one should proclaim:
"All you sentient beings, you should all receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts."
If one sees cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, or any other kind of animal, one should mentally reflect and verbally say:
"You are an animal; arouse the bodhicitta.
Thus, when a Bodhisattva enters any mountain forest, river valley, or wilderness, they cause all sentient beings therein to arouse the bodhicitta.
If this Bodhisattva does not teach and transform sentient beings, they commit a minor transgression.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
You must constantly practice teaching and transformation, giving rise to a heart of great compassion."

When entering the home of a wealthy lay patron, one must not stand among the assembly to preach the Dharma to the white-robed laity; rather, one should sit upon a high seat before the assembly of laypeople.
A Dharma-preaching bhikṣu must not stand upon the ground while preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
When preaching the Dharma, the Dharma-preacher shall occupy a high seat and be honored with incense and flowers, while the fourfold assembly of listeners shall sit on lower seats.
Just as one should be filial and obedient toward one’s parents and respectful and compliant toward the teachings of one’s teachers, like a Brahmin who serves the sacrificial fire;
if the one who preaches the Dharma does not act in accordance with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

All those who have received the Buddha’s precepts with a faithful heart—including kings, crown princes, officials, and disciples of the fourfold assembly—if, out of self-reliance on their own high status, they destroy the Buddha-dharma and its precepts, openly establishing restrictive laws to govern my fourfold assembly, forbidding them from leaving home to practice the Way, and likewise forbidding the creation of images, stupas, sutras, or the Vinaya, they commit the sin of destroying the Triple Gem."
If one intentionally acts as a destroyer of the Dharma, they commit a minor offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha!

If you have left the household life with a sincere heart, yet for the sake of fame and profit, you preach the precepts of the Seven Buddhas before kings and high officials, and recklessly engage in acts of binding and restricting Bhikṣus, Bhikṣuṇīs, and Bodhisattva disciples—this is like a worm within a lion’s body eating the lion’s own flesh; it is not something that external paths or celestial Māras can destroy."
One who has received the Buddha’s precepts should protect them as if thinking of an only child or serving one's parents.

When a bodhisattva hears an outsider or an evil person revile the Buddha’s precepts with wicked words, it is no different from having three hundred spears pierce their heart or being struck by a thousand swords and ten thousand clubs upon their body.
It would be better to enter hell oneself for a hundred kalpas than to hear even once the sound of evil words that break the Buddha's precepts, let alone breaking the Buddha's precepts oneself.
To teach others to create the causes and conditions for breaking the Dharma is likewise devoid of filial piety.
If one intentionally commits [any of these], one incurs a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).
Thus, these nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart.
"O Sons of the Buddha!..."
These are the forty-eight minor precepts!
You all should receive and uphold them.
All bodhisattvas of the past have recited them; all bodhisattvas of the future shall recite them; and all bodhisattvas of the present are now reciting them.
"Listen attentively, O sons of the Buddha!

These ten grave and forty-eight light precepts have been recited by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those of the past, those of the future, and those of the present—and I now likewise recite them."

All of you in this great assembly—whether kings, princes, or officials; bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, or laywomen—who have received and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts, should receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this scroll of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature precepts, so that they may circulate through the three periods of time for all sentient beings, transforming them without end.

One shall behold a thousand Buddhas, each extending a hand to receive one; from life to life, one shall not fall into the evil realms or the eight difficulties, but shall always be born among humans or in the heavens.
Now, beneath this tree, I briefly expound the Dharma-precepts of the Seven Buddhas.
"You all should single-mindedly study the Prātimokṣa and joyfully practice it,
as is explained in detail in each instance within the 'Exhortation to Study' in the Chapter on the Devarāja Animitta."

The three thousand scholars who were seated there listening at that time, upon hearing the Buddha recite this himself, received it with every thought of their hearts, receiving and upholding it with leaping joy.

At that moment, Śākyamuni Buddha finished preaching the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts within the Chapter on the Mind-Ground Dharma Gate of Vairocana Buddha in the World of the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury.

The hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis also spoke thus; from the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara to this site of the Bodhi tree, throughout these ten stages of abiding where they preached the Dharma, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and an inexpressible multitude, they likewise caused them to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning.

In thousands of billions of worlds—the Lotus Treasury World, the World of Micro-dusts, and all worlds—having completed the teaching of all Buddhas’ Treasury of Mind, Treasury of Earth, Treasury of Precepts, Treasury of Immeasurable Vows and Practices, and the Treasury of the Ever-abiding Buddha-nature of Cause and Effect, as well as the treasury of all dharmas spoken by all Buddhas in accordance with Suchness.

Throughout the worlds of hundreds of thousands of millions, all sentient beings receive, uphold, and joyfully practice this, which extensively reveals the characteristics and manifestations of the mind-ground,
as explained in the "Flower-Light King" chapter of the Buddha’s teachings.
The wise person, strong in patience and wisdom, Is able to uphold such a Dharma as this.
Until they attain the Buddha-way, They will securely obtain five kinds of benefits:
First, the Buddhas of the ten directions Will compassionately regard and constantly protect them;
Second, at the time of death, one possesses right view and a joyful mind;
third, in every place of rebirth, one becomes a friend to all bodhisattvas;
fourth, as a mass of merit, one fully accomplishes the perfection of ethical discipline.
Fifth: In future lives, one’s innate precepts, merit, and wisdom will be fulfilled.
This is the sphere of the Buddha’s practice; the wise should contemplate it well.
Those who calculate in terms of a self and cling to signs cannot believe in this Dharma.
For one who has attained the realization of cessation, there is likewise no place for planting seeds;
yet, if one wishes to grow the sprouts of Bodhi and illuminate the world with light,
one should calmly observe the true nature of all phenomena.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither eternal nor interrupted,
neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going—
within such a single mind, one diligently adorns it through skillful means.
What a bodhisattva ought to do should be learned in successive stages;
regarding those in training and those beyond training, one should not give rise to discriminatory thoughts.
This is called the foremost path, and it is also called the Mahāyāna.
All bases of conceptual proliferation are entirely extinguished from this place;
all the *sarvajñā* of the Buddhas emerge from this place.
Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, you should rouse great courage and vigor.
Regarding the pure precepts of all Buddhas, one should protect and uphold them like a bright pearl.
All Bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this;
those of the future shall train in it, and those of the present are training in it now.
This is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity, praised by the Holy Lord.
Having followed his teaching, I have spoken of this immeasurable mass of merit;
I dedicate it to all sentient beings, that we may together proceed toward omniscience.
May those who hear this Dharma swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.
*The Brahmajāla Sūtra, Spoken by Vairocana Buddha, Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva’s Precepts on the Ground of the Mind, Part Two.*
